The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific components of the density, thereby yielding the corresponding weights. A new algorithm is introduced to efficiently capture the desired prior and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, successfully replicating known results from literature and a recent exact strong-coupling analysis. A key finding involved a discrete derivative operator that yields finite parts of two-loop amplitudes or correlators from higher-divergent structures. This operator effectively removes the UV divergences at two loops for the fundamental four-point correlator of outer-valence operators. Furthermore, an alternative representation was developed for the two-loop remainder function in a physical region, leveraging a nonlocal operator along the boundary of the external legs. This format reveals a strong analogy to the four-parton amplitude in conformal field theory, particularly in the limit where the points approach the collinear limit.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAR runtime environment, designed for C++ SMMO applications and featuring object orientation abstractions, automatic memory management, and DynaSOAR Abstract Syntax Trees (DSA) to optimize memory access and allocation.  As a result, we observed substantial performance enhancements, with our prototype achieving up to 10x speed improvements over the conventional CPU implementation and up to 40x speed gains compared to the GPU reference.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn and Fe adatoms on the Nb(110) surface were conducted, involving the Nb d-orbitals in the calculation of local electronic structures. The results demonstrate that the orbital composition of the YSR states is influenced by the crystal field, the arrangement of atoms on the substrate, and the presence of the impurity, with spin-polarized local magnetic fields further complicating the situation. The method's accuracy was validated against experimental data for Mn and Fe adatoms on Nb(110), as well as previous studies of Fe on Pb(111) and Cu on Al(100). The findings offer a detailed understanding of Local Tunneling Spectroscopy measurements and the Local Tunneling Density of States in YSR states.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP, we demonstrate that FourierMask can achieve competitive performance in inference speed, mask resolution, and segmentation quality. Our method surpasses Mask R-CNN with 4x faster inference speed on MS COCO, and achieves the highest resolution masks. Furthermore, FourierMask delivers exceptional performance on medical image segmentation tasks, surpassing traditional architectures like U-Net with better efficiency and mask detail.

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to recent research involving the construction of bounded, flat disks, and it answers a previously asked question about the frequency spectrum of certain surfaces. Additionally, this study demonstrates the precision of its results by showing counter-examples and a new method for identifying essential frequencies.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key characteristics of these core regions and their relationship to the clouds' overall structure. Our modeling suggests that traditional optically thick core sizes correlate with the distance between the cloud's surface and its furthest point. This insight may lead to more accurate future retrievals by focusing on specific cloud features rather than all possible directions.

We investigated how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. The target's plasma density profile significantly influences this interaction, especially in the infrared range, where a square envelope is not adequate due to its steep edges. The effects of a frequency-stretched Gaussian laser pulse on the transmission through the plasma and the resulting ion acceleration were analyzed using 2D and 3D simulations in comparison to experimental data obtained with a Ti:sapphire laser. The results show that lower frequency thresholds of the plasma density profile enable more efficient ion acceleration, characterized by higher energies and narrower energy distributions. The optimal characteristics of this profile depend on the laser intensity, and the effects of frequency stretching are most pronounced at high intensities ($10^{19}$ W/cm$^2$) utilized in heavy ion drivers. The results indicate that transmitting a high-intensity, frequency-stretched laser pulse through a critical density threshold requires a plasma with negative frequency stretching. The effects of a frequency-stretched laser and different plasma density profiles on ion acceleration were examined using simulations, which reveal that for a given intensity, increasing the frequency spread reduces ion energies back to the energies achieved with an unchirped laser. The optimal profile transmission results in ion energies up to two times greater than unchirped transmission.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, it lies between TOI-712 b and d at distances of approximately $0.73$ and $11.6$ astronomical units. Due to TOI-712's youthful age, its inner planets may still be undergoing formation, making TOI-71 d, located within the habitable zone, an interesting target for future study to understand its potential atmospheric composition.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency to replace titanium atoms and exhibit ferromagnetic properties, with possible spin configurations including up/up and down/down.  Specifically, carbon and nitrogen atoms form bonds with two titanium atoms in an anti-ferromagnetic state, with possible spin configurations including up/down and down/up.  However, in the case of carbon, nitrogen can also replace titanium atoms in a down/down state in a semi-conducting state.  To overcome this, we proposed co-doping TiO2 with C, N to achieve a more stable and highly efficient visible-light photocatalyst.  This new material has the potential to catalyze the decomposition of H2O with sunlight.  Initially, we simulated a double substitution in a 96-atom supercell to verify the stability of this new material.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium (ICM) have shown that turbulence and other non-thermal pressures play a significant role in its dynamics. Although simulations are beginning to reflect the temperatures, velocities, and "turbulent" power spectra seen in the ICM, the underlying mechanisms driving this turbulence have not yet been identified. We propose a comprehensive approach incorporating the effects of mergers, AGN feedback, gravity, and thermal processes to understand the turbulent state of the ICM through a self-consistent framework. Utilizing a detailed dataset from a state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulation, we demonstrate how different ICM components interact, revealing that turbulent energy primarily generated by turbulent cascades rather than direct production during the majority of time, with the ICM components exchanging turbulent energy through a similar mechanism to fluid dynamics. We found that while gravitational processes contributed to turbulent pressure, their overall impact is insufficient to account for the observed values. AGN feedback is the dominant driver of turbulent pressure, on average providing 75% of the required support against gravitational forces. The characteristics of this feedback vary, however, presenting further examination.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained with the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey, revealed notable variations in the density structure of gas within this area. By employing a source decomposition technique, we identified 1.4 million individual sources, spanning in brightness temperature from 25 to 870 $\mu$m and listed in the APEX Telescope Imaging Galactic Plane Extended (TIGGA) catalog. A comparison between the 870 $\mu$m and 450 $\mu$m continuum maps, created from HIPO survey data, allowed us to determine the effective sizes of these sources, with a majority appearing compact and regular in shape, despite some irregular high-mass sources still being present. When comparing the linear sizes of sources to their peak flux differences, a standard size-brightness relation was found to hold for most source populations, including those with masses in excess of a certain threshold, similar to observations in other nearby molecular cloud regions, which suggests a degree of universality in the physical properties of small, dense sources. However, when analyzing the physical density distribution within these sources, an increase in peak density with larger source size was found, similar to the density structure present in other areas, indicating that small, dense sources in the CMZ may share common physical characteristics with their counterparts elsewhere in the

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on analyzing blinking patterns in eyes, rather than entire faces. We have collected and analyzed a large dataset comprising 290 subjects with confirmed Bell's Palsy and 579 healthy subjects, utilizing a unique annotation system. This framework divides the problem into two distinct categories: classifying normal and abnormal blinking events, and identifying the specific eye associated with each event. Our innovative approach allows for an early and private diagnosis of Bell's Palsy by analyzing a person's eyes separately from their identity. Furthermore, our results demonstrate improved accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our simplified model achieves a significant 21.7% reduction in accuracy compared to complex systems that analyze entire faces, indicating that Bell's Palsy can be effectively diagnosed by examining eye movements alone.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits and qudrits are successful up to a significantly higher level of noise compared to their qubit counterparts. Additionally, our research explores the impact of measuring local and nonlocal operators on the results.

By combining relativistic classical dynamics with quantum electrodynamics, 
we investigate the polarization of positrons produced during laser-solid 
interactions at intense levels. These positrons hold promise for various 
applications, including polarization-sensitive medical imaging, physics 
research, and biological studies. To accurately assess positron 
polarization, we examine both longitudinal and transverse components of the 
spin. Notably, our findings reveal that a intense circularly polarized laser 
can impart significant positron polarization. The degree of polarization is 
found to be influenced by several key factors, such as the electron and 
nucleus velocities, their initial conditions, and the direction of the 
nuclear velocity in relation to the laser. In fact, varying the direction of 
the nuclear velocity can result in the production of positrons with 
oppositely directed spins. Additionally, our research identifies methods for 
generating highly polarized positron beams from relativistic heavy ion 
targets using only intense lasers. The degree of positron polarization is 
also found to be more substantial in transverse direction compared to its 
longitudinal counterpart.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V, and an extremely compact silicon area of 0.027$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an extremely linear response curve.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including understanding how the nature of the flow might be irreversible. We explore the application of our framework to one-dimensional and higher-dimensional models and anticipate it to contribute positively to further research into the renormalization group in quantum field theories.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

This PhD research focuses on establishing a connection between invariant forms of a principal bundle over a Lie groupoid and the cohomology of its associated Lie groupoid. To achieve this, a connection and a curvature are defined on principal bundles over Lie groupoids within a categorical setting. Notably, a curvature functor from the category of principal bundles to the Lie groupoid is constructed, and its connection to the invariant forms of the Lie groupoid is explored through the Chern-Weil map. Additionally, the relationship between this map and a secondary form derived from a connection and its curvature on a principal bundle over a Lie groupoid is demonstrated.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting distinction between cores that are active in infrared and those that are starless.  Protostellar cores are found to be significantly more massive than their starless counterparts, with no overlap in mass.  Additionally, there is no core type that is marginally massive.  A slight excess of cores, specifically protostellar and transitional, is found to be associated with elevated masses.  To better understand this, the mass distribution is modeled, with the outcome indicating that the excess of massive cores is best explicable by a distinct, highly massive core population.  This discovery raises questions about the characteristics and collapse timescale of this core population, which will be a focus of future research.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple feature extraction techniques, spanning traditional statistics to complex RPFM methods, and showcase improved classification outcomes using a publicly accessible outdoor LiDAR dataset.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

To fully comprehend the origins of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, researchers need to also study high-energy neutrinos and accelerate a next-generation neutrino detector to do so. We present an initial concept for such a detector, called FARA, which would be built into the Shafranovskiy Radio Telescope (SRT) in Chelyabinsk, Russia. The FARA project involves integrating a high-energy neutrino detector into the existing SRT structure with a minimal impact on the telescope's operations. The detector consists of 192 custom-designed digital electronic modules, or readout channels, which are grouped into 8 panels that fit within the telescope's structural supports. Each readout channel includes components such as a cryogenic amplifier, an ADC, and necessary control elements to minimize data transmission while maximizing detection efficiency. The electronic system includes 8 separate power supply units that operate independently to ensure optimal performance. Each panel contains a high-density circuit board containing all necessary components to function correctly. The electronic system includes a sophisticated software system to control and monitor the detector's performance. Each panel contains a custom-designed processing unit to ensure efficient data transmission and minimal latency. The electronic system includes a sophisticated software system to control and monitor the detector's performance, which runs on a Linux operating system and includes a web-based interface to monitor the detector's performance in real-time.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new, empirically based "Einstein type" viscosity approach to address stress calculations during the stick-slip regime.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined and unfixed modes. For a highly elastic membrane, additional steady pattern formations are observed through the competition between centrifugal and pressure forces, as well as a mathematical examination of mode stability.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its non-decreasing nature during expansion, consistent with the second law of thermodynamics.

Researchers have identified the presence of two specific isomers of ethynyl benzene, also known as acetylene benzene or the aglycone of holosetin, in the infrared spectrum of the comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. This discovery required analyzing a complex and highly absorbent spectrum, a task that would have been improbable without prior knowledge. Column densities for these compounds have been estimated at approximately 1.5 times 10 to the power of 4 molecules per square centimeter, suggesting a mixed lineage with a consistent ratio when compared to amine alcohol, as a normalizer.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies this model and enables it to consistently intersect the dark matter curve within a margin of $10^{-4} \text{ to } 10^{-2}$ GeV, by utilizing a previously established dark matter-dilaton scalar interaction and its corresponding connection to the quintessence field. The model's evolution is studied and its parameters are constrained via an extensive analysis of type Ia supernovae, cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations, and Hubble constant data. The results indicate that the model is consistent with the $\Lambda$CDM model while providing new physical insights, with the viscosity coefficient falling within the range $9.14^+0.79_{-0.62} \times 10^{-12}$ and $6.06^+0.42_{-0.38} \times 10^{-12}$ according to two statistical methods. The model predicts a current dark energy equation of state of $-0.99$ and a Hubble constant of $67.24$ km/s/hMpc. The quintessence field's behavior is analyzed and its potential is found

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a desire to acquire new knowledge.  However, existing research on curiosity has mostly focused on its psychological aspects and cognitive development.  There is a pressing need to examine curiosity from a different perspective - that of skill development.  This research aims to explore and define curiosity from this perspective and develop a measurement tool to assess it.  Our proposed model posits that curiosity is influenced by two primary factors - a desire to learn and the belief that one is capable of learning.  This model also suggests that these two factors operate independently and can be measured without interdependence.  A new scale, called the Curiosity Skill Scale (CSS), was designed to assess curiosity based on this model.  The CSS was tested using data from 500 university students and demonstrated validity through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis.  The results confirmed that the CSS can effectively measure curiosity from a skill development perspective.  This research provides a new framework for understanding curiosity that can be applied in educational settings and has implications for curriculum design and instructional practices.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures.

The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowd-sourcing, but they often fall short due to high maintenance costs, limited coverage areas, and insufficient data on road conditions within urban environments. A new approach based on wireless devices utilized by mobile users within the urban area is proposed, taking advantage of their extensive deployment and ability to collect roadside status data through channel measurements, thereby offering a thorough assessment of urban road conditions. A key challenge arising from this approach is the unpredictable variability of mobile devices' trajectories, which can result in inaccurate monitoring outcomes. To address this issue, a cooperative sensing framework is developed to reliably monitor urban roads by coordinating communication and sensing resources among mobile devices. Through strategic allocation of sensing and communication resources, the system maximizes the minimum combined coverage and accuracy of monitoring across the urban road network. Numerical analysis validates framework effectiveness and illustrates its potential for precise road condition evaluation.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on energy scales, with the strongest limits being 12.8 GeV for dark matter scenarios. Additionally, we considered specific extensions to the effective field theory, including the sterile neutrino and dark matter scenarios. For instance, we found that in a specific dark matter scenario, J/ψ decay into invisible matter can produce energy scale lower bounds as high as 16.6 GeV. Notably, in certain cases where the energy scale is below 2.5 GeV, the J/ψ invisible decay width is predicted to be within the J/ψ total width uncertainty.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated and that they tend to misjudge the importance of various essay components, consequently assigning excessive weight to certain features. Candidates have also discovered that employing statistically insignificant but highly influential features can significantly increase predicted scores. In response, our study aims to investigate the potential for controlling the level of bias in these automated scoring models, with an emphasis on maintaining high accuracy while reducing bias. We developed several methods to regulate the degree of control exerted by the algorithm, allowing us to experiment with various approaches. Our results indicate that it is possible to create relatively unbiased scoring algorithms with comparable performance to their biased counterparts. Moreover, we propose the use of regularisation terms as an effective means of controlling and adjusting the degree of bias in these algorithms.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a 2-stage nucleus detection algorithm, designed to address cancer diagnosis. It begins with a fully automatic step, where the information extraction process is streamlined, thus reducing the need for manual annotation. Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and a special orthogonal group or a symplectic group over this field. We establish a condition under which two irreducible, non-self-dual generic representations, that share the same Bessel model type, become isomorphic. Additionally, we provide an explicit criterion for the equality of two generic representations acting on a specific class including self-dual ones, utilizing Cartier models and a criterion introduced by S. B. Roy for Bessel models.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is initiated by NLRP3 inflammasome assembly as a response to cellular stress caused by the infection with SARS-CoV-2.  This process is further driven by the viral protein NSP12's activation of Caspase-1 through its unique 'coronin activity'.  A small molecule designed based on the transition state of the inflammasome can halt pyroptosis and limit the excessive inflammation associated with severe COVID-19.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a unified perspective on various types of graph convolutions. This new perspective facilitates the analysis of how information flows and limits through the different parts of a GCNN, including the graph sparse connectivity, graph convolutions, pooling operations, and fully connected layers. We validate our findings through detailed numerical analyses of information flow and limitations within the Node Classification task.
